p.title: How Do Electoral Incentives Affect Legislator Behavior? Evidence from U.S. State Legislatures

ext.title: Fouirnaies and Hall: Electoral Incentives and Legislator Behavior
authors: Alexander Fouirnaies (University of Chicago, Harris School)
ext.venue: American Political Science Review 116(2): 662-676. First published online 27 Sep 2021. Metadata hint confirmed against the PDF's first page; no correction needed.
ext.document_type: Journal article, empirical, open access (CC BY 4.0). Text file has journal pagination 662-676 (PDF page N = journal page N+661).
ext.coverage: Read all 1,927 lines of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\cdf16c0e1139.txt (main text, Tables 1-5, Figures 1-2, conclusion, references). Not in the text file: the Appendix (Tables A.1 and A.3, Figures A.3-A.4, the Alt-Bueno de Mesquita-Rose model review, interest-group detail), supplementary material, and the Dataverse replication files (doi 10.7910/DVN/LHTRWM). Appendix-dependent claims are reported only as the main text describes them. Annotations: all 46 items in C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\cdf16c0e1139.json were read. All are type Highlight, all have empty content (no sticky-note text), and colours are green, yellow or pink with no stated meaning. The file is the only annotation file for this PDF. Covered text is paraphrased below, not quoted, to respect the one-quote limit; the verbatim text is in the JSON. Some covered-text fragments begin mid-word from rect edges (items 3, 15, 16, 18). Topics present: electoral accountability, term limits, lobbying and interest groups (as a mechanism and as ratings source), committee assignments. Absent: network analysis, path-finding, allocation frontiers, persuasion or turnout, and text-as-data measurement (bills were collected, but no text model is used).
ext.research_question: Do electoral incentives change how legislators allocate effort to visible activities (bill sponsorship, committee service, floor attendance), and do they change ideological positioning? The paper uses term limits as the source of variation in incentives.
ext.theory: Electoral accountability models (Alt, Bueno de Mesquita and Rose 2011, reviewed in the Appendix): voters cannot observe competence directly and infer it from observable effort, so reelection-minded incumbents should allocate more effort to visible activities. Removing reelection incentives (term-limited final term) should reduce that effort. For ideology, the paper contrasts the marginality hypothesis (Fiorina 1973; Downs-style moderation), ideological shirking (Bender and Lott 1996), pandering (Canes-Wrone, Herron and Shotts 2001) and citizen-candidate models (fixed positions). Null ideological effects are read as consistent with citizen-candidate models and with voter inattention to platforms (p.671-674).
ext.data: Sample: legislator-term panel from 14 U.S. states whose legislatures have term limits of three or more terms (16 chambers: 14 houses plus the AZ and ME senates; Table 1, p.665). Nebraska (unicameral) and staggered-term senates are excluded. Coverage ranges by state (e.g., AZ 1991-2016, OH 2007-2014; Table 1). Outcome samples (Tables 2-4): roll-call attendance N=11,109 legislator-terms, 4,642 legislators; bills N=16,727, 6,207 legislators; committee activity N=16,255, 6,123 legislators (Table 4). Additional controls for Table 3 col 4: New York and Texas (non-term-limited), matched synthetic controls, N=11,416, 1,506 legislators. Scale: about 780,000 bills, over 16 million roll-call votes linked to candidates, about 6,200 legislators, and over 80,000 interest-group ratings (intro and abstract, p.662-663). Data were hand-collected from official state sources, about 100 hours per state (p.665). Election returns from Klarner et al. (2013), cleaned in Fouirnaies and Hall (2018).
ext.method: OLS difference-in-differences at the individual level (eq. 3, p.669): Productivity_ict = beta * TermLimited_ict + alpha_i + delta_ct + eps_ict, with legislator fixed effects and chamber-year (or chamber-party-year) fixed effects; robust SEs clustered by legislator. Outcome is a PCA-based productivity index (first principal component of log bills sponsored, a committee activity index, and percent of floor votes cast; normalized mean 0, SD 1; p.667). Committee index weights: 0 non-member, 1 member, 2 vice chair, 3 chair, summed across committees (eq. 1-2, p.666). Ideology: W-NOMINATE first dimension, absolute value as extremity, and party-split W-NOMINATE (Table 5, p.673). Interest-group ratings (0-100) across abortion, business, education, environment, guns, taxes, labor unions and an "other" category, estimated with legislator-by-group and group-by-chamber-year fixed effects (eq. 4, p.672). Robustness: log seniority, seniority FE, cohort-year FE, and matched NY/TX synthetic controls with match-pair-year FE (Table 3, p.670).
ext.identification: Within-person comparison: each incumbent's change in effort on entering the binding final term is compared with contemporaneous legislators in the same chamber-year who are not yet termed out, which holds fixed time-invariant individual type (Alt et al. selection problem, p.664-665). The authors note that standard leads/pretrend tests are not feasible because treated legislators have few periods (p.669), so they rely on robustness checks instead. Threats addressed: seniority/learning (log seniority, seniority FE, cohort-year FE), anticipation of own future termination and mean reversion (matched NY/TX controls with the same number of terms served, p.670 and fn 13). Heterogeneity predicted by theory (lifetime vs consecutive limits, professionalism, salary) is used as validation (p.671).
ext.scope: Population: state legislators in 14 term-limited states (16 chambers), U.S., roughly 1991-2016, low-salience state legislative elections. Institution: term limits of three or more terms. Authors argue state legislatures resemble others on key attributes (Mooney 2009), so effects may generalize (p.663), but only 14 of 99 legislatures are covered (p.665). They explicitly disclaim normative conclusions about term limits as policy and aggregate legislative effort (p.674).

key_findings.finding: Termed-out (final-term) legislators have lower legislative productivity index, the main outcome. The effect is about one-quarter SD and is unchanged with chamber-party-year FE.
key_findings.numbers: Term limited = -0.24 (SE 0.03) in both columns; N=11,109; 4,642 legislators; outcome SD 1.00

key_findings.finding: Effect is robust to alternative counterfactuals. It shrinks with seniority controls but stays negative and significant. It is larger with matched NY/TX controls, which address both learning and anticipation.
key_findings.numbers: Log(seniority) -0.23 (SE 0.03); seniority FE -0.09 (0.03); cohort-year FE -0.09 (0.03); matched NY/TX -0.41 (0.03), N=11,416, 1,506 legislators

key_findings.finding: Floor attendance falls in the final term. Abstention rises from about 10% to 12.7% of votes, a proportional increase of about 27%. The authors say the effect is meaningfully larger than the term-length effect in Titiunik (2016).
key_findings.numbers: Percentage of floor votes = -2.70 (SE 0.53); -2.63 with party-year FE; outcome mean 90.48

key_findings.finding: Bill sponsorship falls in the final term, about 6% in proportional terms.
key_findings.numbers: Sponsored bills = -1.63 (SE 0.77) and -1.34 (SE 0.70) against mean 27.32; N=16,727; 6,207 legislators

key_findings.finding: Committee activity falls in the final term, about 8% in proportional terms.
key_findings.numbers: Committee activity = -0.31 (SE 0.06) and -0.30 (SE 0.05) against mean 3.84; N=16,255; 6,123 legislators

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity fits theory. Effects are larger under lifetime limits than consecutive limits, in more professionalized legislatures, and where salaries are higher. Effects are also larger in California and Oklahoma, where limits are cumulative.
key_findings.location: Appendix Table A.3, summarized in text p.671 (table not in extracted text)
key_findings.numbers: No numeric values in main text

key_findings.finding: Estimates are probably a lower bound, because some termed-out legislators run for other offices and keep electoral incentives. Effects remain large in other term-limited states.
key_findings.numbers: No numeric values in main text

key_findings.finding: Descriptively, legislators who serve their final term are less productive than legislators in earlier terms. Survivors to a third term are also more productive on average, which the authors treat as selection.
key_findings.numbers: Figure 1 values are in the figure; no numeric values in text

key_findings.finding: Ideological extremity (absolute W-NOMINATE) does not systematically change in the final term. The overall coefficient is marginally significant and small. Party-split coefficients are indistinguishable from zero.
key_findings.numbers: |W-NOMINATE| = 0.02 (SE 0.01), N=4,356, outcome mean 0.63; W-NOMINATE Dem column (mean -0.62) = -0.00 (SE 0.01), N=2,192; Rep column (mean 0.52) = -0.01 (SE 0.02), N=2,143. Column identities for the party split are inferred from the outcome means.

key_findings.finding: Interest-group ratings show no systematic shift in issue positions for either party across the seven issue areas plus other.
key_findings.numbers: Most point estimates fall between 0 and 1 percentage point on a 0-100 scale, and are statistically indistinguishable from zero (figure values not in text)

key_findings.finding: Headline interpretation. Elections shift effort toward observable productivity but not ideological positioning. The authors argue the mechanisms are unresolved and could involve voter attention, party or interest-group influence.

measures: Legislator productivity index: first PCA component of (log) bills sponsored, committee activity index, and percent of floor votes participated (p.666-667).

Committee activity index: 0 non-member, 1 member, 2 vice chair, 3 chair, summed over committees in a chamber-term; weights admitted to be somewhat arbitrary but results claimed not to depend on them (p.666).
Bills sponsored per legislator-term; data show mean 27 per year, SD 30 across legislators, within-legislator SD 17 (p.666).
Floor-vote participation: share of roll calls with a recorded yes or no vote (p.667). Some states record only final-passage votes (p.667).
Ideology: W-NOMINATE first dimension (negative = liberal, positive = conservative), absolute value as extremity (p.668). Party-split W-NOMINATE (Table 5).

Interest-group ratings: percent of votes aligned with a group's position, from Project Vote Smart or group sites, for abortion, business, education, environment, guns, taxes, labor unions, and other (p.672).

Treatment: TermLimited = final term before a binding term limit. Term-limit type (lifetime vs consecutive vs cumulative) and state professionalism/salary are heterogeneity moderators (Appendix Table A.3, p.671).
limitations: Parallel-trend and lead/pretrend diagnostics are not feasible given the small fixed number of periods for treated legislators (p.669).

Controls are less senior than the treated legislators; if productivity-seniority is concave, estimates overstate the effect (p.668-669). Log-seniority, seniority FE and cohort-year FE partly address this, but at a cost to functional-form assumptions (p.670).
Control legislators may anticipate their own future term limits, which would bias the comparison (p.670). Mean reversion may also contribute to the within-state estimate (fn 13, p.670).
Party control over committee assignments and bill coordination means effects may partly reflect party strategy rather than individual choice (p.666).
Half of the term-limited states cap bill introductions, though not stringently (p.666). Roll-call recording differs across states (p.667), though comparisons are within chamber-term.
Data collection is manual and labor-intensive (about 100 hours per state), limiting coverage to 14 of 99 legislatures (p.665).
Termed-out legislators may still face electoral incentives through other offices, which attenuates estimates (p.671).

W-NOMINATE is coarse and may miss issue-specific shifts. Interest-group ratings only detect systematic shifts, not heterogeneous individual deviations (p.674). Groups select bills for their own agendas (p.672).

The paper cannot say whether freed-up time goes to leisure or constituent service, or what happens to aggregate legislative effort (p.674). Mechanisms (voter attention, party, interest groups) are not identified (p.675).
Normative conclusions about term limits are explicitly disclaimed (p.674). Appendix content (Tables A.1, A.3; Figures A.3-A.4) is not in the extracted text and is unverified here.

short_quotes.quote: Elections appear to induce incumbents to allocate their effort toward observable measures of productivity

paul_markup.text: Abstract finding: term-limited legislators sponsor fewer bills, are less productive on committees, and miss more floor votes.
Intro: prior work gives plausible reasons to doubt electoral incentives' power in many settings.
Abstract conclusion: elections shape effort even in low-salience settings but less so ideological positioning (fragment starts at rect edge).
Data allow fine-grained measures of how incumbents allocate effort.
Summary: termed-out legislators sponsor fewer bills, do less committee service, and attend fewer votes.
Multiple DiD designs give consistent evidence for the effects of electoral incentives.
Null ideology result fits a view where voters are poorly informed about candidate positions.
Elections in state legislatures are an important tool for shaping effort, against the view that low-salience elections leave legislators unconstrained (fragment).
Term-limit debate was well funded and has produced a deep academic literature.
Candidate moderation is weaker in state legislative elections than federal ones.
Consistent with voter inattention to state legislators' own behavior.
Threat of reelection can change officeholder actions even when outcomes do not depend on their ideology or effort.
Mechanisms of democracy seen in term-limited legislatures should generalize to other electoral contexts.
Low salience and low voter information make state legislatures a hard test of accountability models (fragment).
Prior designs (Besley and Case; List and Sturm) use within-state variation in lame-duck governors.
Lame-duck selection could produce an offsetting positive difference, biasing estimates down (fragment).
Alt, Bueno de Mesquita and Rose design assumes the type distribution of first-term governors is unchanged when the limit is extended.
Ferraz and Finan restrict the sample to barely-winning first-term mayors who win a second term.
Design requires non-staggered terms, so several state senates are excluded.
Hypothesis: incentives push legislators to observable effort to sway voter inferences.
Missing roll-call votes is one of the most basic forms of legislator shirking.
Legislators' webpages commonly list committee service and bills introduced, as advertising.
Committee effects should not be read as purely individual, since party assigns committees.
Bill sponsorship stats: mean 27 per legislator-year, SD 30 across legislators, 17 within.
Bill-level dataset records sponsor, name, summary, and whether the bill became law.
Over 16 million individual roll-call votes linked to specific candidates.
Cross-state differences in roll-call availability do not affect results because comparisons are within chamber and term.
Ideology is scaled with the W-NOMINATE algorithm.
W-NOMINATE sign convention: negative is more liberal, positive is more conservative.
Main estimate is a decrease of about one-quarter SD in the productivity index, across all three components.
Log-seniority specification keeps comparisons within legislatures but imposes a parametric form.
Anticipation concern: legislators who will be termed out may change effort in early terms.
New York and Texas chosen as non-term-limited control states, straightforward to digitize.
Committee activity index falls about 0.3 points from a mean of 3.8, roughly 8% proportionally.
Lifetime limits weaken incentives more, and the estimate is larger in those states, as expected.
Section heading: termed-out legislators do not seem to shift platforms.
First column outcome is the absolute value of W-NOMINATE.
Interest-group scores of issue-specific voting used to test ideological shifts.
Data reshaped so each row is a legislator ranked by interest group in a term.
Conclusion: electoral incentives influence how legislators allocate effort in important ways.
Elections induce effort toward observable productivity; once term-limited, legislators sponsor fewer bills and attend fewer votes.
Candidate moderation and election outcomes are muted in state legislatures.
Term-limit critique: final-term shirking by incumbents who no longer need reelection.
Caveat: freed-up time could go to leisure or to other constituent service, so shirking is not established.
Caution: findings are not a basis for the normative term-limit debate; they show how elections shape reelection-minded behavior.

rel.summary_md:
Fouirnaies and Hall use term limits in 14 U.S. state legislatures (16 chambers, roughly 1991-2016) to ask whether reelection incentives change what legislators do. They compare each incumbent's binding final term with that same person's earlier terms, against same-chamber-year colleagues, using legislator and chamber-year fixed effects. In the final term, a PCA productivity index falls by 0.24 SD (N=11,109 legislator-terms). The drop ranges from -0.09 with seniority fixed effects to -0.41 with matched NY/TX controls. Roll-call participation falls 2.7 points from a mean of 90.5, bill sponsorship falls about 6% (-1.63 from a mean of 27.3 bills), and committee activity falls about 8%. Ideology does not move. |W-NOMINATE| changes by +0.02, the party-split estimates are about 0, and interest-group ratings across seven issue areas show no systematic shift. The authors read this as elections shaping visible effort, not positions. They add that legislators who leave to run for another office keep their electoral incentives, so the estimates are a lower bound.

For Paul's system, the paper matters in four places. (1) The receptivity layer cites it for a 0.60 "less responsive" multiplier on retiring members. The paper measured effort, not responsiveness to pressure. Its null on positions argues against reading the drop as movability, and its footnote 14 contradicts the retiring list, which includes members running for other office. (2) Several measures treat roll-call participation and sponsorship volume as dispositions or costly signals: diligence, the C criterion, the agenda volume and say-do path A. The paper shows these move with electoral status inside the same person. (3) The paper finds that effort and position separate cleanly, which supports keeping influence and alignment on separate axes. (4) Prospective test H2 cites this paper, but under it, retiring members' reduced activity can produce a correlation with no responsiveness behind it. The evidence comes from state legislatures with exogenous, binding limits. In Congress, retirement is voluntary and self-selected, so the effect transfers only weakly.

bearings.paper_claim: Removing reelection incentives lowers visible effort: the productivity index falls -0.24 SD (SE 0.03), with a range of -0.09 to -0.41 across specifications. Ideological positioning does not shift: |W-NOMINATE| +0.02 (SE 0.01), the party-split estimates are about 0, and interest-group ratings show no systematic change. Legislators who run for other offices keep their electoral incentives, so the estimates are a lower bound.
bearings.paper_location: Tables 2-3 p.669-670; Table 5 p.673; Figure 2 p.674; text and fn 14 p.671
bearings.system_side: incent_mult = 0.60 for every member on fec/retiring_members.txt. The docstring calls final-term members less responsive to pressure and cites Fouirnaies & Hall, and the factor enters pressure_mult = clip(susc*incent*pt, 0.50, 1.60). The list header says it 'Includes members seeking OTHER office (Golden/Barr/Stefanik etc.)', and Andy Barr is the first entry. Line 129 also attributes the competitiveness term 1+.30(comp-0.5) to Fouirnaies-Hall, but the paper does not test seat competitiveness at all.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak for the 0.60 size and the 'responsiveness' reading. The paper estimates effort allocation in low-salience state chambers under exogenous, binding term limits. It does not estimate response to lobbying or money, and its null on positions points against extra movability or immovability. Congressional retirement is voluntary and self-selected, which is the confound the paper's within-person design is built to avoid. Its footnote 14 directly contradicts treating members who seek other office as having no electoral incentive. The direction (less effort in the final term) carries over; the magnitude and the mechanism of 'pressure response' do not.

bearings.paper_claim: Floor-vote participation is state-dependent within the same legislator. It falls 2.70 points (SE 0.53) from a mean of 90.48 in the final term, about a 27% proportional rise in abstention. Committee activity falls about 8% (-0.31 from 3.84).
bearings.system_side: diligence_z is the mean of z-log votes_cast within chamber (with a full-term guard at 25% of the chamber median) and LEP follow-through. It is labelled a C-role disposition and enters susceptibility at -0.20. Members on the retiring list therefore get lower diligence and higher susc, which partly offsets their incent 0.60. Electoral status enters the pressure term twice, with opposite signs, and is never modelled explicitly.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Moderate. Missing votes is a universal congressional behaviour, and the paper's within-person identification is cleaner than anything the system has. However, the state final-term drop of about 3 points is small next to the cross-member spread in congressional votes_cast. It matters most for members in their final Congress, or those campaigning for another office, whose absences are campaign-driven. The disposition reading holds only after electoral status is held fixed.

bearings.paper_claim: Roll-call participation moves with electoral incentives inside the same person (-2.70 points in the final term, mean 90.48). As a criterion it therefore mixes trait and electoral situation.
bearings.paper_location: Table 4 p.671; p.666 (missing votes as basic shirking)
bearings.system_side: The interview-genre C criterion is a Spearman correlation between C and votes_cast (recorded PASS, rho +0.155), computed cross-sectionally with no stratum for electoral status (retiring or running for other office).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak to moderate. The PASS is recorded and must not be re-run (single-look). The paper shows the criterion has a situational component, so any external claim from this look should carry an UNSTRATIFIED label on electoral status. This matters most if campaign-driven absences correlate with interview volume, for example among members running statewide.

bearings.paper_claim: In the final term, effort falls (sponsorship -6%, committee activity -8%, participation -2.7 points) while positions stay flat (W-NOMINATE and interest-group nulls).
bearings.system_side: Under the protocol, H2 (labelled Byrne/F&H) tests Spearman(frozen pressure_mult, |overall-tier movement|) after the freeze. pressure_mult carries the 0.60 retiring factor. Tier movement depends on new evidence events, and retiring members produce fewer of them under this paper's effect, so a positive H2 could arise mechanically from lower activity rather than from responsiveness. The paper also predicts no true position change from the F&H channel.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Moderate as a threat to interpretation. It applies only if tier movement is driven by evidence volume. If the contract is still unfrozen, a reported retiring/other-office stratum could be added. If it is frozen, any H2 result should carry this caveat. This is analysis, not a look, and stays UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Bill sponsorship volume falls about 6% when reelection incentives end (-1.63, SE 0.77, mean 27.32; N=16,727) with no ideological change. Sponsorship volume partly reflects electoral advertising (legislators' webpages list bills introduced) rather than position.
bearings.paper_location: Table 4 cols 3-4 p.671; p.666; Table 5 p.673
bearings.system_side: Agenda is an unnormalized volume sum: signed contribution times |topic weight| over all selected rows, then PERCENTRANK. A member's final-Congress drop in activity therefore lowers Leg% with no change in stance. The design keeps stance as a separate signed multiplier, which matches the paper's finding that effort and position separate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The 6% effect at the state level is small, and in Congress it would touch only members in their final Congress or those running for other office. The paper supports the influence-vs-alignment split. It does not address the 4:2:1 role weights or cosponsorship.

bearings.paper_claim: Sponsorship is effort directed at voters' inferences, not a revelation of position: it falls when reelection ends while ideology stays flat. Legislators advertise bills introduced on their webpages.
bearings.paper_location: p.666 (advertising, observable-effort hypothesis); Table 4 p.671; Table 5 p.673
bearings.system_side: Path A treats an authored or original-cosponsored bill in the category as the costly signal that corroborates Champion or Defender. The overall gate's thin_high_volume rule (at least 10 direct bills with no more than 20% advanced) treats high-volume introduction as cheap talk.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The paper supports the thin_high_volume reading, since introduction volume responds to electoral display. It also cautions that path A sponsorship is partly advertising, though a bill signed in the CU direction is still more than talk. The evidence comes from state legislatures with bill-introduction caps in half the states (p.666), and the paper does not test whether a bill's direction corroborates rhetoric.

gaps_exposed: Retiring list conflates members leaving office with members seeking other office (header of fec/retiring_members.txt, which is the system's own label); the paper (fn 14, p.671) says the latter keep electoral incentives. There is no field separating the two.

No electoral-status control on participation- or volume-based measures (diligence_z votes_cast, Leg% agenda volume, rank-honors rate per service year, congress-activity counts). A member's final Congress or a statewide campaign mechanically lowers them.
The 0.60 incent_mult is unestimated, and the paper offers no estimate of responsiveness to lobbying or money for final-term members. It estimates effort only, and finds positions unchanged.
Retiring status enters susceptibility twice with opposite signs: incent 0.60 lowers pressure, while lower diligence (from more missed votes) raises susc. This interaction is undocumented.
The system has no within-member, cross-Congress design for effort measures. The paper's identification relies on legislator fixed effects, while all system measures are cross-sectional.
The prospective H2 contract has no reported stratum for retiring or running-for-other-office members, so activity-volume artefacts can pass as responsiveness.
flags: CITATION MISATTRIBUTION: fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:129 calls 1+.30*(comp-0.5) 'The Fouirnaies-Hall competitiveness term'. The paper studies binding term limits only and never tests seat competitiveness. The term is neutral under COMPET_MULT (default ON, D-107) but still live when COMPET_MULT=0.

CONFLICT WITH THE PAPER: fec/retiring_members.txt includes members seeking other office (for example Barr, listed first) under the Fouirnaies-Hall final-term rationale. The paper (fn 14, p.671) says such members retain electoral incentives.

OVER-READING: the receptivity docstring (receptivity_layer.py:15-16) says final-term members reduce 'effort/responsiveness'. The paper shows reduced effort and NO change in position or ideology. Responsiveness to pressure is an extrapolation, not a finding.

Pooled-coefficient wording: the paper's -0.24 SD is a pooled estimate across 16 chambers with documented heterogeneity (lifetime vs consecutive limits, professionalism, salary; Appendix Table A.3, not in the extracted text). Quote it with those strata or label it UNSTRATIFIED. The window is about 1991-2016 and the denominator is legislator-terms (N=11,109).
No REJECTED SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges, per-edge volume normalization) is argued by this paper. No LDA edge or weight use (D-021). No reciprocity claim (D-104..D-108).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's annotation record for this paper is empty: no takeaways, system links or anchor, only 46 uncommented highlights. His component positions cite the paper for the legislative pillar, say-do gate, rank honors, receptivity layer, behavioural dispositions, activity score and prospective contract, and they read it as 'observable effort is an incentive-sensitive signal.' The evidence agrees with that reading. His highlights also stress the parts that cut against how the system uses the paper. He highlighted the ideology null, the voter-inattention reading and the caution that freed time may go to constituent service, so shirking is not established. Those points undercut the receptivity layer's 'less responsive to pressure' gloss. He also highlighted that sponsorship and committee service are advertised on webpages, which makes sponsorship partly display rather than a pure costly signal. His notes are stale relative to the system in two ways. They do not record that the retiring list includes candidates for other office, which the paper's lower-bound argument flags. They also do not record that the competitiveness term attributed to this paper is now neutral under COMPET_MULT, and was never tested by it.

related.why: Fouirnaies & Hall rely on individual-level two-way fixed-effects DiD with a staggered final-term treatment and admit they cannot run pretrend tests (p.669). Imai & Kim's critique of TWFE causal assumptions applies directly when judging how far the -0.24 SD estimate should transfer.

Ramey links conscientiousness to sponsorship. Fouirnaies & Hall show sponsorship and participation also move with electoral incentive inside the same person, a situational confound for any trait reading of those behaviours (diligence_z, the C criterion).

The two are sibling factors in the receptivity layer: Fouirnaies & Hall drive incent_mult 0.60 and Linde & Vis drive pt_mult. Both condition on electoral situation, and the code notes they share an input (security drives both incent and pt).

Both papers study U.S. state legislatures. Bucchianeri's state-level effectiveness scores are the outcome-side counterpart to Fouirnaies & Hall's effort index, and would show whether final-term effort losses reduce effectiveness.
Fouirnaies & Hall's ideology null rests on W-NOMINATE scaling of state roll calls, which is the NOMINATE family Poole reviews. The scaling's coarseness is the paper's own stated limitation (p.674).
